summary: 中考 reading round 2: final check of the corrected passages (+canaries) in groups, 2 finders + 2 verifiers per group

findings.proposed: to learn more about the bacterium.
findings.reason: The pronoun has no clear antecedent and does not agree. The nearest noun phrase is the plural “the bacteria” (now “the bacteria” after the man-made correction), so singular “it” either mismatches it or seems to point to “the environment”. Question 15 shows the intended meaning: “further research on the bacterium”. Naming the noun fixes both the agreement and the reference.

va.why: "It" has a valid singular antecedent: the act of introducing the bacteria into the environment, which the preceding "which could be harmful" also refers to. It can also be read as the article's overall topic, the bacterium. Either way the sentence is grammatical and clear in context, and the exam has the same wording. Naming the noun is a clarity preference, not a definite error.

vb.why: The nearest noun is plural "the bacteria", so singular "it" either mismatches it or seems to point to "the environment". A careful teacher would mark this unclear pronoun. Question 15 ("further research on the bacterium") confirms the meaning, and the passage uses "bacterium" for the species throughout. "learn more about the bacterium" fixes both the agreement and the reference without changing the meaning.

findings.reason: A number plus unit used as a hyphenated compound modifier before a noun takes the singular unit: 100-meter world record. The exam paper also has 100-meter.

findings.current: Picking tomatoes is easy work for humans.
findings.proposed: Picking tomatoes is tiring work for humans.
findings.reason: The next sentence says robots “can help with it”, which only makes sense if the work is hard. The exam paper has “tiring work”, so “easy” contradicts the context.

findings.current: whether there is any tomatoes hidden behind leaves
findings.proposed: whether there are any tomatoes hidden behind leaves
findings.reason: The verb does not agree with its subject: “there is” + plural “tomatoes”. The header says the correction to “there are any tomatoes” was applied, but the text has only half of it: the noun was made plural and the verb was left singular.
The present perfect needs the past participle “fallen”, not the past tense “fell”. The exam paper has “has fallen”.

va.why: The current text matches. Before a noun, a hyphenated number-plus-unit modifier takes the singular unit, so it should be "100-meter world record". The exam dump also has "100-meter".
The current text matches. "Easy work" contradicts "Now farming robots can help with it". The exam dump has "tiring work".

The current text matches. "There is" does not agree with plural "tomatoes". The header says the applied correction was "there are any tomatoes", so only half of it got into the text. The fix finishes that correction.
The current text matches. The present perfect needs the past participle: "has fallen". The exam dump has "has fallen a lot".

vb.why: When a number and unit form a hyphenated modifier before a noun, the unit stays singular, so it should be "100-meter world record". The exam dump also prints "100-meter".
"easy work" contradicts the next sentence, "Now farming robots can help with it", which assumes the job is hard. The exam dump has "tiring work". This is a definite logic error.

"there is any tomatoes" is a subject-verb agreement error. The header says the correction was "there are any tomatoes", but only the noun was made plural. It needs the full form: "whether there are any tomatoes hidden behind leaves".
The present perfect needs the past participle: "has fallen". "has fell" is a definite grammar error, and the exam dump has "has fallen".
